title: Why tellers matter
hookLine: a story lives because someone tells it well and truly

lines: A STORY AT THE END OF DINNER.
cards: A grandmother at the end of a family dinner, telling how she came to this country. The grandkids have heard it before. One of them corrects a detail; she waves it off and keeps going.
Years later she's gone, and that grandkid is the one at the end of the table, telling it to the next lot. Some details are different now. Is it still her story?
Whether a story survives depends less on the story than on the people who keep telling it. Today: katha.

teach.h: KATHA: THE TELLING IN THE GURDWARA.
teach.b: Sikhs have a word for the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani in the gurdwara: katha. A katha teacher sits before the sangat, takes a line, and opens it up with stories and pictures.
Bhai Gurdas did a version of that in verse, carrying the Guru's teaching in the language of the fields and the bazaar, so people could hold on to it.
Bhai Nand Lal did it in Persian, for listeners who loved that kind of poetry. That's why this block has called them tellers. Two words carry today's lesson: well and truly.
They pull in different directions, and a good teller holds both.

teach.h: WELL: THE STORY HAS TO LAND.
teach.b: Well means the story has to land; if nobody can follow it, it dies with the teller. Yesterday's sandalwood and bamboo is told well.

Truly means the teller doesn't bend the story to look good, or to win an argument. And telling well can tempt you away from telling truly: a detail gets bigger with each retelling because it gets a better reaction.
That's why, starting next week, this path reads the janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, carefully.
Different tellers told them differently, and the Sikhs who kept them have had to think about which tellings to trust. One more thing.
Every Sikh who explains the Guru's teaching to a child at a kitchen table is a teller too.
The chain didn't stop with Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal. It runs through any household that passes the stories on.

how: In gurdwaras, katha is the spoken explanation of Gurbani: a teacher takes a line and opens it with stories, often drawing on Bhai Gurdas and the sakhis of the Gurus.

o: the daily reading of the Guru's command
a hymn sung by the ragis with instruments
the spoken telling of Gurbani in the gurdwara

p: the spoken telling in the gurdwara
land it, and don't bend it

s: a story that's told well is always told truly
telling well can tempt a teller to make a detail bigger each time.
the janamsakhis come in different tellings

games.q: you're retelling a family story, and one detail always gets a big laugh, though it didn't quite happen that way. what do you do?
o: keep the laugh: that's how it's told now.
tell it as it really happened.
stop telling the story at all.
games.why: today's line is tell it true: a story needs telling well to live, and telling truly to stay itself.

practice: Choose a story you've told more than once, from your family, your work, your own life, and run it through the way you usually tell it.

Then run it again and listen for the places where it's grown, the bit made a little funnier, a little bigger, a little kinder to yourself, and just notice where the true version is. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.

wordCard.voice: Katha, the spoken telling and explaining of Gurbani in the gurdwara, kept alive and true the way Bhai Gurdas and Bhai Nand Lal told it.

carryVoice: Your line: tell it true. Told well to live, told truly to stay itself. That's seven hundred twenty days.
